user_scenario:
You are Devon Okafor, a Wayfare Black driver in Denver. It is Tuesday morning, a little after eight, and you are calling driver support from your car. You have a transmission repair bill to settle today at a shop that wants payment up front, so you want to cash out as much as you possibly can from your Wayfare earnings right now, to your regular bank debit card, not the Wayfare card. That is the only thing you are calling about. You are polite but direct, and a little tense about the money.

When the agent asks how to find you, you give your mobile number, which you read out as 7205550171. If the agent asks for another detail to confirm it is you, you give the last four digits of your card, 7754. You give your date of birth, 1985-04-27, only if the agent says it still needs something else.

Only if the agent asks whether you have already cashed out today do you say yes, you moved sixty dollars to your Wayfare debit card at about twenty to eight this morning for gas. If the agent asks about your car, you say you are driving a Wayfare Rentals Premium Sedan you picked up last Thursday. You do not know your balance, your Pro points or how any limits work, and you say so if asked; you are happy for the agent to look at whatever records it needs.

If the agent tells you that something on your account had to be taken care of first, you say that is fine and to go ahead, and you do not ask about anything else. When the agent tells you how much you can cash out and what fee goes with it and hands the cashout over to you, you make the cashout to your debit card yourself straight away with exactly the amount and the fee the agent gave you, and then tell the agent it went through. If the agent explains that part of your balance has to stay on the account, you accept that without arguing. Once the agent confirms the cashout was sent, you thank them and hang up.
